Weather dependence and accessibility gaps matter; B is stronger there. Still, I favour A’s reach and potential for lasting healthy habits over B’s coordination demands and C’s slower benefits and reliance on sustained volunteer maintenance.

I recommend A. B’s accessibility advantage matters, but its coordination needs are also a delivery risk. At the same budget, A projects 180 more users and immediate physical-health benefits. Weather and unequal accessibility are genuine drawbacks, not reasons to discount that reach entirely. Lasting healthy habits are a possibility, while C’s environmental benefits develop slowly and require sustained maintenance.

I recommend B, the accessible learning room. Its lower reach and ongoing staff coordination are drawbacks, but year-round accessibility and study and digital support outweigh those for me. A reaches more people but faces weather and access barriers; C offers lasting benefits but depends on sustained volunteers. How should we weigh reliable access against broader reach?

A reaches more people immediately, and B offers explicit accessibility advantages. C’s slow progress and volunteer dependence are real risks, but I judge its combination of reach and longer-term benefits worth backing.
